title: What good children’s social care looks like — prevention, market pressures and workforce
label: 21 October 2026 · Children’s social care evidence session
summary: Charities NSPCC, Action for Children and Barnardo’s told the committee that a good children’s social care system focuses on prevention, supports safe family life where possible, provides the right foster or residential care for children with complex needs, and gives sustained help after reunification. They warned the current system spends most money on crisis care, is strained by a shrinking foster pool and a growth in adolescents with complex needs, and faces market problems such as a dominant private residential sector and slow registration processes. They urged investment in early help, better support for kinship carers and foster carers, clearer rules and capacity to regulate unregistered homes, and inspection that follows children’s life trajectories and relationships.

chapters.title: What 'good' children’s social care looks like
chapters.takeaway: A good system is prevention-focused, treats children in care like any other child, and supports them into adulthood.

turns.speaker: Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson
turns.text: What are the hallmarks of a good social care system for children in care—what should it aim for?

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: These children are legally 'children of the state'—the state becomes their parent and should have the same hopes for them as any parent: safety, the right home, steady care, good schooling and long-term support into adulthood.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: We back the Families First model: keep children safely at home where possible, support kinship carers, prioritise fostering for most children, but accept fostering won't suit every child—residential care must be genuinely therapeutic for those with complex needs.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: Prevention is central. Right now the system spends most money on crisis responses instead of early help; that means children reach harm before services intervene. We must invest earlier to stop escalation.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Also, inspect and measure children’s progress over time, not just a snapshot—capture their life at school, at home and in the community so we can judge real change.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: And listen properly to children. Doing that well—especially for children with communication or complex needs—is hard but essential to understand their experience.

chapters.title: Prevention, reunification and funding pressures
chapters.takeaway: The charities argue we must spend more on early help and sustained post-return support to avoid repeated crises and costly returns to care.

turns.speaker: Lord Johnson of Marylebone
turns.text: Was there a policy change or drift that created today’s pressures?

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: It’s drift. Market shaping was weak for years. The system was left to evolve without national oversight, so supply, costs and practice didn't adapt to the current cohort of older, more complex children.

turns.speaker: Lord Johnson of Marylebone
turns.text: How much of the rise in older children is due to unaccompanied asylum-seeking children?

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: About 9% of children in care are UASC. They affect the adolescent numbers, but they’re not the whole story; other extra-familial harms and adolescent needs have increased too.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: We spend around 80% of children’s social care funding on crisis work. Early help funding has fallen about 40% in 10 years. That imbalance drives rising costs and poor outcomes.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: On reunification, breaking returns cost around £300m a year, while investing properly in post-return support might cost about £67m—there’s a clear economic case for longer-term investment.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Local authorities want to support reunification but need resources and national guidance; over one in five children who return to families re-enter care within a year, which shows current support is often too short.

chapters.title: Residential care market: private dominance, geography and co-operatives
chapters.takeaway: Residential care has shifted to private providers, causing distance from home, variable quality and pressure when fostering falls short.

turns.speaker: Lord Faulkner of Worcester
turns.text: Why is residential care more expensive and why are those numbers growing while foster places fall?

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Children in homes often arrive after failed foster placements and have higher, complex needs; homes must be therapeutic and well matched, which costs more than standard fostering does.

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: About 80% of children’s homes are run by the private sector. We've also lost over 7,000 foster carers in four years. The private sector tends to buy cheaper property—so many homes sit far from children’s communities.

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: Regional care co-operatives could improve joint planning and block buying, but they risk favouring large providers and pushing small local providers out, and they may split commissioning of care away from local family support.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: Don’t see residential care in isolation—placement pressure reflects lack of upstream prevention. Families need continuing support whether a child is in care or not.

turns.speaker: Baroness Pidgeon
turns.text: Do you have the numbers on how many homes are charity-run, local authority or private?

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: I can check exact counts, but the private sector runs about 80% of homes; the north-west has four times as many homes as London, creating long-distance placements.

chapters.title: Unregistered homes, registration backlog and practical fixes
chapters.takeaway: Unregistered settings risk safety and isolation; charities want clearer distinctions, temporary registration and faster processing for trusted providers.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: What extra risks do unregistered children’s homes pose and what should be done?

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Unregistered homes can lack proper building safety, trained staff, vetting and therapeutic input; they may increase exploitation risks. But we must distinguish 'trusted providers awaiting registration' from fly-by-night operators.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Action for Children recommends a temporary registration route for reputable providers on a clear path to registration, plus fast-tracking trusted voluntary providers.

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: Some unregistered placements exist only because there’s nowhere else to put a child. That is not acceptable—capacity and sufficiency must be fixed so emergency or inappropriate placements stop.

turns.speaker: Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson
turns.text: How long does registration take in practice?

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: It varies. If there are no planning problems and paperwork and a registered manager are in place, it can take about 12 weeks. Often planning permissions and local issues slow things down.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Some practical changes would help: allow transfer of registered managers between settings, fast-track voluntary sector providers, and clear triage of registration backlogs.

chapters.title: Fostering, kinship, workforce training and inspection
chapters.takeaway: Recruitment and retention of diverse foster carers, fair pay/allowances, kinship support, workforce training for complex needs, and an Ofsted framework focused on children’s trajectories are priorities.

turns.speaker: Baroness Watkins of Tavistock
turns.text: What do you make of government plans for fostering and kinship care?

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: A national foster campaign is welcome. We need more diversity among carers, better retention, and practical changes such as default delegated authority for carers and housing policy that creates spare rooms.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: Kinship pilots are promising, especially where carers get non-means-tested allowances, but that creates a two-tier system while pilots run. Paid employment leave for kinship carers—similar to adoption leave—needs serious consideration.

turns.speaker: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley
turns.text: Is training adequate for rising complex needs?

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: No. We need more specialist skills on neglect, infant and baby development, attachment and child sexual abuse indicators. Practitioners must be confident to judge and act without waiting for disclosures or 'persistence' in neglect.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Chittlehampton
turns.text: Is there a training approach that keeps high expectations while managing severe needs?

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: We don't have one single scheme to name. Inspections should recognise small but vital progress (e.g. a child learning mealtime behaviour) as foundations for bigger gains, and inspectors need training to see that.

turns.speaker: Baroness Redfern
turns.text: How bad are workforce retention and multiple social workers per child?

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: Recruitment and retention are major problems; 24% of children had three or more social workers in a year. The Families First design could reduce handovers, but implementation must protect skills and not raise thresholds that remove early help.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: The residential workforce also needs qualification and CPD reform; DfE has commissioned a review and we hope it strengthens training and career pathways.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What should Ofsted prioritise in the new inspection framework?

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: We welcome the new evaluation areas—especially 'enduring relationships'—but Ofsted should assess children’s life trajectories rather than snapshots, be proactive about engaging diverse children’s voices, and help services improve between inspections.

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: Ofsted should work closely with system reforms so inspections and policy pull in the same direction. Try using 'young inspectors'—children who can bring direct perspective to reviews.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: Three inspection priorities: check how services include babies' needs and voices, test whether prevention is stopping escalation, and evaluate the quality of reunification planning and post-return support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send us any follow-up data you mentioned on UASC numbers, residential home counts and good reunification examples.

turns.speaker: Jessica Ford
turns.text: We will follow up with the requested data and examples.

turns.speaker: Nicola Smith
turns.text: We'll also supply figures on Barnardo’s residential provision and any relevant research on local variation.

turns.speaker: Eavan Mckay
turns.text: We will share case studies and the evidence behind our points on neglect and reunification economics.
